q: You deploy a custom Linux container to Azure App Service. The app inside listens on port 8000, and the site returns errors because App Service cannot reach it. What should you configure?
o: Set the WEBSITES_PORT app setting to 8000
Set the PORT environment variable inside the Dockerfile to 80
Enable Always On
Set WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE to true
e: For custom containers, WEBSITES_PORT tells App Service which container port to route requests to; by default App Service tries to detect ports 80 and 8080. Changing an environment variable inside the image does not change where App Service forwards traffic, Always On keeps the app loaded but does not fix routing, and the storage setting controls the shared /home directory.

q: A containerized Node.js app on App Service needs a value called DB_HOST. You add DB_HOST as an app setting in the portal. How does the code read it?
o: As an environment variable named DB_HOST inside the container
From a file at /home/site/appsettings.json that App Service generates
Only through the App Service REST API at runtime
It can't; app settings apply only to code-based apps, not containers
e: App Service injects app settings into the container as environment variables, so the code reads process.env.DB_HOST (or the equivalent in other languages). No settings file is generated for this purpose, no REST call is needed, and custom containers support app settings the same way code-based apps do.

q: Your App Service container needs a database password that is stored as the secret DbPassword in the key vault contoso-kv. You don't want the value stored in app settings. What should you put in the app setting?
o: @Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=contoso-kv;SecretName=DbPassword)
keyvaultref:https://contoso-kv.vault.azure.net/secrets/DbPassword
${secrets.DbPassword}
$(KeyVault:contoso-kv:DbPassword)
e: App Service resolves Key Vault references written as @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) or @Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=...;SecretName=...), using the app's managed identity. The keyvaultref: format belongs to Azure Container Apps secrets, and the other two are not recognized syntaxes, so App Service would pass them through as plain text.

q: You want an App Service app to pull its container image from Azure Container Registry without storing registry credentials. Which two steps are required? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.
o: Enable a managed identity on the app and grant it the AcrPull role on the registry
Set acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true in the app's site configuration
Enable the registry admin user and copy its password into DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_PASSWORD
Grant the managed identity the Key Vault Secrets User role on the registry
e: App Service can authenticate to ACR with a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity: the identity needs AcrPull on the registry, and the site configuration must tell App Service to use managed identity credentials (acrUseManagedIdentityCreds). The admin user is exactly the stored credential you wanted to avoid, and Key Vault roles have no effect on registry access.

q: An app uses a user-assigned managed identity to pull from ACR, but image pulls fail with an authorization error. The identity has AcrPull, and acrUseManagedIdentityCreds is true. What is the most likely missing setting?
o: acrUserManagedIdentityID set to the identity's client ID
WEBSITES_PORT set to 443 so the image pull uses HTTPS
keyVaultReferenceIdentity set to the user-assigned identity
Always On set to true so the identity token stays valid
e: When acrUseManagedIdentityCreds is true and no user-assigned identity is specified, App Service uses the system-assigned identity. To use a user-assigned identity you must also set acrUserManagedIdentityID to that identity's client ID. The port, Key Vault reference identity, and Always On settings have nothing to do with image pull authentication.

q: An app setting uses @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://contoso-kv.vault.azure.net/secrets/ApiKey/) with no version. The secret is rotated and a new version is created. What happens?
o: The app picks up the latest version automatically, within 24 hours
The app keeps the old value until the reference is edited to include the new version ID
The app restarts immediately when the new version is created
The reference stops resolving because a version is required
e: If the reference omits the secret version, App Service uses the latest version and refreshes cached Key Vault reference values every 24 hours, so a rotated secret is picked up within that window without a redeploy. A reference that includes a version stays pinned to that version. App Service does not restart on every new version, and versionless references are valid.

q: Your app has both a system-assigned and a user-assigned managed identity. Key Vault references must be resolved with the user-assigned identity, which is the only one granted access to the vault. What should you configure?
o: Set keyVaultReferenceIdentity to the user-assigned identity's resource ID
Add the identity's client ID to every Key Vault reference string in the settings
Disable the system-assigned identity so App Service switches automatically
Set acrUserManagedIdentityID to the client ID of the user-assigned identity
e: Key Vault references use the system-assigned identity by default. To use a user-assigned identity, set the keyVaultReferenceIdentity property (for example with az webapp update --set keyVaultReferenceIdentity=<identity resource ID>). The reference syntax has no client ID field, and acrUserManagedIdentityID only affects image pulls from ACR.

q: A key vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Which role should you assign to an App Service managed identity so that it can resolve Key Vault references for secrets, with least privilege?
o: Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Administrator
Key Vault Secrets Officer
Contributor on the key vault
e: Key Vault Secrets User allows reading secret contents, which is all a Key Vault reference needs. Secrets Officer can also create and delete secrets, Administrator has full data-plane control, and Contributor is a management-plane role that does not grant reading secret values under the RBAC model. Least privilege points to Secrets User.

q: On App Service for Linux, your custom container writes temporary files to /home, and you notice that the files are shared between all scaled-out instances. You want each instance to use only its own local storage. What should you do?
o: Set WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE to false
Set WEBSITES_PORT to 0 so /home isn't mounted
Scale in to one instance so only one container writes to /home
Enable a sidecar container that owns the /home directory
e: For Linux containers, if WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE isn't specified, the /home directory is shared across scaled instances by default; setting it to false disables that sharing. WEBSITES_PORT controls request routing, scaling in removes redundancy rather than changing storage behavior, and a sidecar adds another container without changing /home.

q: Your team pushes contoso.azurecr.io/web:prod after every release and wants the App Service app to pull and restart with the new image automatically. What should you enable?
o: Continuous deployment from ACR, which uses a registry webhook to notify App Service
A timer-triggered ACR task that restarts the web app after each push
A retention policy on the registry so App Service always finds only the newest prod image
Health check on the App Service app, which pulls the image again when it changes
e: App Service supports CI/CD from Container Registry: when enabled, a webhook on the registry notifies App Service when the configured image tag is pushed, and App Service pulls the new image and restarts. ACR tasks can't restart a web app by themselves, retention policies only clean up untagged manifests, and health check monitors instances without changing their image.

q: A custom container on App Service fails to start, and you need to see its stdout and stderr output, including the startup logs. What should you do?
o: Turn on container logging (file system) in App Service logs, then open the log stream
Open the registry webhook history, which records the container's startup output
Run kubectl logs against the App Service plan that hosts the container
Query the ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL table in the Log Analytics workspace linked to the app
e: App Service captures container output once container logging is enabled in App Service logs, and you can then view it through the log stream or download it. Registry webhooks don't record container output, kubectl only works against Kubernetes clusters, and ContainerAppConsoleLogs is the table for Azure Container Apps, not App Service.

q: You converted an App Service app to a sidecar-enabled custom container app. You notice that changes to WEBSITES_PORT and DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_USERNAME no longer have any effect. Why?
o: They don't apply to sidecar apps; each container is configured in its sitecontainers definition
Sidecar-enabled apps read container settings only from Key Vault references, never from app settings
App Service ignores all app settings after a restart until the plan is scaled
The settings must be prefixed with SIDECAR_ for each container in a sidecar-enabled app
e: For apps that aren't sidecar-enabled, the main container is configured through app settings such as DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_URL, DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_USERNAME, DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_PASSWORD, and WEBSITES_PORT. For sidecar-enabled apps those settings don't apply; each container, its port, and its image-pull authentication are defined as Microsoft.Web/sites/sitecontainers resources.

q: You want an App Service app setting called FeatureColor to take its value from the key App:Color in Azure App Configuration, without changing application code. Which configuration is correct?
o: @Microsoft.AppConfiguration(Endpoint=...; Key=App:Color), with App Configuration Data Reader for the app
Copy the value from App Configuration into the app setting in every deployment pipeline run
@Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=contoso;SecretName=App-Color), pointing the reference at the App Configuration store
Grant the app the App Configuration Reader role and read the value from the REST API at startup
e: App Service and Functions support App Configuration references in app settings; they resolve with the app's managed identity, which needs the App Configuration Data Reader data-plane role. Copying values during deployment drifts out of date, Key Vault references only point at Key Vault, and App Configuration Reader is a control-plane role that does not grant access to key-values.

q: A container app uses the default revision mode. You deploy a new image and the new revision fails its health probes. What happens to production traffic?
o: Traffic stays on the old revision until the new one is running and healthy
Traffic is split 50/50 between the old and new revisions while probes retry
Traffic moves to the new revision immediately, and the app starts returning errors
Both revisions are deactivated until you redeploy a working image
e: Single revision mode is the default. New revisions are provisioned and scaled, and traffic is diverted from the old revision only once the new replicas are running; if an update fails, traffic remains on the old revision and old revisions are deprovisioned automatically after a successful switch. Traffic splitting requires multiple revision mode.

q: You want to send 10 percent of requests to a new revision of a container app and keep 90 percent on the current revision. What must you configure?
o: Use multiple revision mode and set traffic weights of 90 and 10
Keep single revision mode and set maxReplicas to 10 on the new revision
Create a second container app and put Azure Front Door in front
Add a revision label called canary; labels get 10 percent of traffic
e: Traffic splitting requires multiple revision mode, and the combined weight of all traffic rules must equal 100 percent. Replica counts don't control traffic share, and labels give a revision its own FQDN without requiring any traffic weight. A second app with Front Door works but is unnecessary when Container Apps supports weighted splitting natively.

q: Which change to a container app creates a new revision?
o: Changing a container image or an environment variable
Adding a new secret to the configuration section
Changing the ingress target port in the configuration section
Switching the revision mode from single to multiple
e: Revision-scope changes are changes to the properties.template section, such as container images, environment variables, scale rules, and the revision suffix, and they create a new revision. Application-scope changes in properties.configuration, such as secrets, ingress, registry credentials, and revision mode, apply to all revisions without creating a new one.

q: In a blue-green rollout, the green revision should receive no production traffic, but testers must call it directly. What should you use?
o: Label the revision green and have testers call its label FQDN
Give the green revision a traffic weight of 1 percent for testers
Put the green revision in a different Container Apps environment
Expose the green revision through a Kubernetes NodePort service
e: A revision label gets its own FQDN (app name, three dashes, and label), so testers can reach a specific revision directly while its traffic weight stays at 0 percent. A 1 percent weight would still send real users to it, a separate environment is a separate deployment, and NodePort is a Kubernetes concept that Container Apps doesn't expose.

q: Your blue-green pipeline needs predictable revision names such as myapp--v2-3-0 so it can set traffic weights by name. What should the pipeline set on each deployment?
o: template.revisionSuffix to a value that identifies the release
configuration.activeRevisionsMode set to single for every release
A new secret named after the release version
maxInactiveRevisions set to 0 so old names are freed
e: Setting template.revisionSuffix gives deterministic revision names in the form <app>--<suffix>, which a pipeline can reference when assigning traffic or labels. Single revision mode disables traffic splitting, secrets are application-scope and don't name revisions, and the inactive revision limit only controls how many old revisions are kept.

q: You run az containerapp revision set-mode --mode multiple on an existing app. What is the effect?
o: Multiple revisions can be active, and the change itself creates no new revision
A new revision is created and immediately receives 100 percent of the app's traffic
All existing revisions are deleted and recreated in multiple mode
Traffic is automatically split evenly across all active revisions of the app
e: Revision mode is an application-scope setting. Changing it with az containerapp revision set-mode controls whether several revisions can be active at once, and Microsoft notes that changing the revision mode doesn't create a new revision. Traffic weights are still yours to configure, and existing revisions are untouched.

q: Two container apps, orders and inventory, run in the same Container Apps environment. Which statement about the environment is correct?
o: They share the environment's virtual network and Log Analytics workspace
Each app gets its own isolated virtual network inside the environment
Apps in one environment must use the same container image and version
Each app must be in its own resource group, separate from the environment
e: An environment is a secure boundary around a group of container apps: apps in the same environment share the same virtual network and send logs to the same logging destination. Each app can use its own images, and resource group placement is independent of environment membership.

q: A new workload needs GPU-capable dedicated hardware while other apps in the same environment should keep scale-to-zero serverless billing. Which environment type supports this?
o: A workload profiles environment: a Dedicated GPU profile plus the Consumption profile
A Consumption-only environment, which assigns dedicated GPU hardware to apps automatically
Two separate AKS clusters, one with GPU nodes and one with spot nodes
A Consumption-only environment with maxReplicas set to 1 for the GPU app
e: Workload profiles environments (the default, v2) support both the Consumption plan and Dedicated workload profiles in the same environment. Consumption-only environments are legacy and run only on-demand Consumption compute, so they can't host dedicated or GPU profiles. AKS isn't required for this scenario.

q: You are creating a workload profiles Container Apps environment in your own virtual network. Which subnet configuration is valid?
o: A dedicated /27 or larger subnet delegated to Microsoft.App/environments
A /29 subnet that is shared with the virtual machines in the network
A /23 or larger subnet that must not be delegated to any service
Any existing subnet; the environment creates its own subnet automatically
e: Workload profiles environments need a dedicated subnet of /27 or larger that is delegated to Microsoft.App/environments. The legacy Consumption-only environment instead requires /23 or larger and must not be delegated. Subnet size can't be changed after the environment is created, so plan it carefully.

q: A container app must read a queue connection string that is stored in Key Vault, using a user-assigned managed identity. How should you define the secret?
o: keyvaultref:<secret URI>,identityref:<identity ID>, used through secretRef
@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=<secret URI>) as the environment variable value
Copy the value into the image at build time and read it as a file
Mount the key vault as an Azure Files volume and read the secret from disk
e: Container Apps secrets can reference Key Vault with the format <name>=keyvaultref:<secret URI>,identityref:<identity resource ID>, and containers consume the secret through an environment variable with secretRef. The @Microsoft.KeyVault syntax is for App Service and Functions, baking secrets into images is insecure, and Key Vault can't be mounted as an Azure Files share.

q: The frontend container app must call the internal-only container app named catalog in the same environment. What is the simplest way to address it?
o: Call it by its app name, such as http://catalog, inside the environment
Use the private IP address of a catalog replica from the environment
Expose catalog with external ingress and call its public FQDN over HTTPS
Create a Kubernetes Service object that points to the catalog pods
e: Container apps in the same environment can call each other by app name, and the environment's DNS resolves it to the app's internal endpoint. Replica IPs change, making catalog external defeats the internal-only requirement, and Container Apps doesn't let you create Kubernetes Service objects directly.

q: After an incident you must roll a container app back to the previous revision immediately. The app is in multiple revision mode, and both revisions are active. What is the fastest safe action?
o: Shift traffic weights: 100 percent to the previous revision, 0 to the faulty one
Delete the container app and redeploy the previous image from the registry
Switch the app to single revision mode so traffic falls back to the older revision
Restart the faulty revision so it reloads the last known-good configuration
e: In multiple revision mode you can shift traffic between active revisions instantly by changing weights, which is the built-in rollback mechanism. Deleting and redeploying causes downtime, switching to single mode keeps traffic on the latest revision, and restarting the faulty revision doesn't remove the bad code.

q: You update the value of a secret that an environment variable references through secretRef. Running replicas still see the old value. Why?
o: Secrets are application-scope; restart the revision or deploy a new one to load it
Secrets are only read when the Container Apps environment itself is recreated
secretRef values are cached for 24 hours, like App Service Key Vault references
The secret's name must change whenever its value changes, so that replicas reload it
e: Secrets live in the application configuration, so updating them doesn't generate a new revision, and existing replicas keep the value they started with until the revision is restarted or a new revision is created. Recreating the environment isn't needed, the 24-hour cache belongs to App Service Key Vault references, and secret names don't need to change.

q: A revision in multiple revision mode is no longer needed, but you want to keep it available for a quick rollback without it consuming resources. What should you do?
o: Deactivate it with az containerapp revision deactivate
Set its traffic weight to 0 percent and leave it active
Delete the container app and keep the image in ACR
Remove its label so it stops running
e: Deactivating a revision stops its replicas so it no longer runs or receives traffic, and it can be activated again later. A revision with 0 percent traffic stays active and can keep replicas running, deleting the app removes everything, and removing a label only removes the label FQDN.
